**ABSTRACT**  
Filipino Sign Language (FSL) is the legally recognized language of the Filipino deaf community under Republic Act 11106, yet practical tools for bridging communication between deaf signers and hearing individuals remain scarce. This study presents a tool called Sikap-Salita which is a web-based system that recognizes FSL signs from video input, translates the recognized text, and produces spoken output in both English and Filipino.Two sign recognition models were trained and compared under identical conditions on the FSL-105 dataset (105 signs, 2,130 video clips). A Bi-Directional Long Short-Term Memory (Bi-LSTM) baseline and a Siformer, a feature-isolated transformer architecture that processes left-hand, right-hand, and body landmarks through separate streams before fusion. Skeletal landmarks were extracted via MediaPipe Holistic (75 keypoints per frame), normalized through re-centering, shoulder-width scaling, and temporal resampling to 64 frames, and augmented with six on-the-fly strategies. In the standard 80/20 test split, the Siformer achieved 96.2% top-1 accuracy and 0.955 macro F1, outperforming the Bi-LSTM baseline at 91.7% top-1 accuracy and 0.908 macro F1. Five-fold cross-validation confirmed the gap, with the Siformer averaging 94.8% (SD 1.2%) against the Bi-LSTM’s 89.9% (SD 1.8%). The recognition pipeline was integrated with NLLB-200 for English-to-Filipino translation and Qwen3-TTS for neural speech synthesis, achieving a mean sign-to-speech latency of 1.8 seconds at 28 to 30 frames per second. A web application built with FastAPI and a browser-based frontend enables real-time skeleton visualization, dwell-based word commitment, sentence building, and bilingual spoken output. End-to-end accuracy reached 94.1% with a false trigger rate of 2.3%. This work represents the first application of the Siformer architecture to FSL, the first controlled baseline comparison on FSL-105 under identical preprocessing, and the first integration of neural TTS with a sign language recognition pipeline for Filipinos.

**Keywords**  
Filipino Sign Language, sign language recognition, Siformer, Bi-LSTM, text-to-speech, MediaPipe Holistic, FSL-105, assistive technology

1. # **INTRODUCTION**

Communication paves the way for how people interact with each other and create meaningful relationships [\[1\]](#bookmark=id.ejb805dqtyg1)[\[2\]](#bookmark=id.mcexywkrgiti). As per Article 19 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR), everyone has the right to freedom of speech and expression as well as to impart information through any forms of media [\[3\]](#bookmark=id.8l3aed7figi6). For persons with disabilities (PWDs), these rights are reinforced by the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD) [\[4\]](#bookmark=id.8t9duk1cx0re). Globally, the World Health Organization estimates that over 430 million people require rehabilitation services for disabling hearing loss, and this figure could exceed 700 million by mid-century [\[5\]](#bookmark=id.qs5px8hq2lwv). Approximately 70 million deaf sign language users face substantial institutional and linguistic barriers [\[2\]](#bookmark=id.mcexywkrgiti). Accessible communication tools are critical for social inclusion, and for access to education, employment, and legal justice [\[1\]](#bookmark=id.ejb805dqtyg1).   
In the Philippines, despite the enactment of RA 11106 (the Filipino Sign Language Act of 2018), the deaf community still encounters significant barriers in healthcare, government services, transportation, employment, and justice — largely due to a shortage of FSL interpreters and specialized tools [\[6\]](#bookmark=id.7t58ne7xzk4k)[\[7\]](#bookmark=id.hsf5vyktez7f)[\[8\]](#bookmark=id.s3zdt641x97h). According to the Department of Health's February 2026 data, 151,459 Filipinos are in the deaf and hard of hearing community [\[9\]](#bookmark=id.kd4s6y3ied1a). FSL has its own distinct grammar, syntax, and morphology, and serves as the mandated communication medium across schools, government transactions, broadcast media, and workplaces [\[10\]](#bookmark=id.l63l9cfzqtrz)[\[11\]](#bookmark=id.1kpid3godhiu).  
Existing assistive technologies from hearing aids to AI-driven systems, have seen significant advancements [\[12\]](#bookmark=id.lhuwynhfxnov). Progress in machine learning and computer vision now allows machines to recognize sign language more effectively, with deep neural architectures including CNNs, LSTMs, and Transformers showing increasingly strong results [\[10\]](#bookmark=id.l63l9cfzqtrz)[\[13\]](#bookmark=id.ag4ort1pazxi). While existing FSL studies have demonstrated promising results, several gaps remain. First, no existing FSL system employs a feature-isolated transformer architecture such as Siformer [\[14\]](#bookmark=id.clrmmqdwurrd). Second, none utilizes the FSL-105 dataset [\[15\]](#bookmark=id.rzy3crsln9uy), the only publicly available labeled FSL video dataset. Third, no FSL system has integrated a neural TTS model with an English-to-Filipino machine translation pipeline. Fourth, no FSL study provides a controlled comparison between a simpler baseline and an advanced architecture under identical conditions.   
With this, this study aims to:

1. extract skeletal landmarks from FSL-105 video clips using MediaPipe Holistic and construct a normalized, augmented dataset;  
2. train and compare a Bi-LSTM baseline and the Siformer under identical conditions, evaluated via top-1/top-5 accuracy, macro F1, and 5-fold cross-validation;  
3. integrate the recognition pipeline with Qwen3-TTS and NLLB-200 for bilingual spoken output; and  
4. develop a FastAPI web application and evaluate end-to-end performance through quantitative metrics and Mean Opinion Score (MOS) evaluation.

Furthermore, this study directly addresses the communication gap hindering the deaf community's autonomy, aligning with UN SDGs 4 (Quality Education), 10 (Reduced Inequalities), and 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities). It contributes to FSL-specific technology research through: (a) the first application of Siformer to FSL, (b) a controlled model comparison as a benchmark for future FSL studies, (c) a reproducible methodology trained on the open-access FSL-105 dataset, and (d) a working prototype integrating recognition, translation, and speech synthesis. The systematic review findings further underscore that user-centered design and responsiveness may be as critical as raw accuracy, an insight that will guide the evaluation of Sikap-Salita's end-to-end user experience [\[16\]](#bookmark=id.tikhbsav50v3).

## **1.1 	Review of Related Literature**

A systematic review of AI-based FSL recognition literature conducted alongside this study surveyed five core FSL studies published between 2022 and 2026, selected through a PICOC-guided appraisal process. The review covered architectural designs, recognition accuracy, real-time deployment, user experience, and FSL-specific linguistic challenges.  
For non-FSL sign languages, existing systems span a range of architectures. For ASL, PopSignAI achieves 82.9% user-independent accuracy using LSTM on 200,000 samples [\[15\]](#bookmark=id.rzy3crsln9uy), while the Mamba Vision Model attains 99.98% for static alphabet classification [\[15\]](#bookmark=id.rzy3crsln9uy). CopyCat combines Hidden Markov Models with pose estimation frameworks for word-level verification at \~90.6% accuracy [\[15\]](#bookmark=id.rzy3crsln9uy). The AI-Based LGP Interpretation System extends recognition to sentence construction via ConvLSTM and ChatGPT, reaching up to 95.6% accuracy [\[15\]](#bookmark=id.rzy3crsln9uy).  
For Filipino Sign Language specifically, the reviewed literature reveals a clear architectural progression. Early systems relied on classical methods such as Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) and Support Vector Machines (SVMs). The current generation is dominated by deep learning, particularly CNN-LSTM hybrids and Transformer-based models. Pilare et al. [\[17\]](#bookmark=id.jxc5444vpwfj) utilized MediaPipe for landmark extraction with a machine learning classifier, recognizing 3 words and 27 phrases, demonstrating that carefully designed pipeline components can achieve practical accuracy even with simpler architectures. Cayme et al. [\[10\]](#bookmark=id.l63l9cfzqtrz) employed CNN-LSTM with MediaPipe on 15 dynamic FSL expressions, integrating lightweight model conversion to reduce computational overhead. Montefalcon et al. [\[18\]](#bookmark=id.coqsy8sii38b) reported 94% LSTM accuracy on 15 continuous FSL phrases.

The highest reported FSL accuracy belongs to the Signify system [\[19\]](#bookmark=id.fsq6o0swqkv4)[\[20\]](#bookmark=id.f5un1vjfnr9b), which compared an LSTM baseline against a Transformer model on the FSL-105 dataset, with the Transformer achieving 98.73% test accuracy — further improved to 99.60% with data augmentation. The TinyFSL project [\[21\]](#bookmark=id.d7vruuvi2zqa) applied knowledge distillation to compress a CNN-Transformer model into a TinyML-compatible format deployable on mobile devices without cloud connectivity, demonstrating that high accuracy can be preserved after compression. KamAI [\[16\]](#bookmark=id.tikhbsav50v3), an Android FSL recognition app using CNN and MediaPipe, achieved 88.38% (letters), 91.41% (numbers), and 83.08% (words) accuracy, with ISO 25010 User Acceptance Testing returning 'Highly Acceptable' ratings across all six quality dimensions: Functionality (4.73/5), Reliability (4.51), Compatibility (4.71), Usability (4.50), Efficiency (4.59), and Portability (4.77). This is the most comprehensive user-centered FSL evaluation to date, although no study has directly benchmarked AI-based FSL systems against live human interpreters in a controlled experiment.

**Table 1\. Summary of Existing AI-Based Sign Language Technologies for FSL**

| Study | Architecture | Key Finding |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Pilare et al. [\[17\]](#bookmark=id.jxc5444vpwfj) (2024) | MediaPipe \+ ML classifier | Recognized 3 words and 27 FSL phrases |
| Cayme et al. [\[10\]](#bookmark=id.l63l9cfzqtrz) (2024) | CNN-LSTM | Real-time recognition of 15 FSL gestures; lightweight deployment |
| TinyFSL – Tipan et al. [\[21\]](#bookmark=id.d7vruuvi2zqa) (2024) | TinyML / 2D CNN \+ Transformer | Compressed SLT model deployable on mobile via knowledge distillation |
| Signify – Ayco et al. [\[19\]](#bookmark=id.fsq6o0swqkv4) (2025) | LSTM \+ Transformer | Transformer achieved 98.73% accuracy on FSL-105; bidirectional S2T and T2S |
| KamAI – Lota et al. [\[16\]](#bookmark=id.tikhbsav50v3) (2025) | CNN \+ MediaPipe | 83–91% accuracy; ISO 25010 UAT 'Highly Acceptable' across all dimensions |

Most recently, Pu et al. [\[14\]](#bookmark=id.clrmmqdwurrd) proposed Siformer, a feature-isolated transformer for skeleton-based sign language recognition that separates left hand, right hand, and body landmark streams before fusing them for classification. Evaluated on WLASL100 (100 ASL signs), Siformer achieved 86.50% top-1 accuracy. Its feature-isolation mechanism handles missing or occluded joints gracefully when one hand leaves the frame, only that stream is affected, making it especially robust for real-world signing conditions.

2. # **METHODOLOGY**

## **2.1 	Materials and Methods**

This study employed an applied experimental research design involving iterative software prototype development followed by quantitative performance evaluation. The core scientific contribution is a controlled comparison between the Bi-LSTM baseline and Siformer under identical data conditions. Development followed five phases: (1) data pipeline construction (landmark extraction, normalization, augmentation); (2) sign recognition model training and comparative evaluation; (3) TTS and translation integration; (4) web application development; and (5) end-to-end system evaluation.

![][image1]  
**Figure 1\. Five Phases of the System Development**

## **2.2 	Procedures**

### *2.2.1 	Data Collection*

This study used the FSL-105 dataset \[15\], the only publicly available labeled FSL video dataset as of March 2026, hosted on Mendeley Data under CC-BY 4.0. The dataset contains 105 FSL signs across 2,130 .MOV video clips (\~4 seconds each, 640×360 resolution), captured on a uniform blue background by a single adult deaf FSL signer reviewed by an FSL expert. Signs span 11 categories (GREETING, SURVIVAL, NUMBER, CALENDAR, DAYS, FAMILY, RELATIONSHIPS, COLOR, FOOD, DRINK), with approximately 20 clips per class and a pre-defined 80/20 split (\~1,525 training / 426 test clips). No additional video data is collected; dataset limitations are addressed through data augmentation.

### *2.2.2  	Data Preprocessing*

![][image2]  
**Figure 2\. Data Preprocessing Steps**

Sikap-Salita adopted a pose-based approach in which raw video is converted to skeletal landmark sequences, eliminating sensitivity to background, lighting, clothing, and skin color, and reducing input dimensionality to 225 values per frame. 

* Step 1 – Landmark Extraction: Each video clip (\~120 frames at 30fps) was processed through MediaPipe Holistic, which outputs 75 landmarks per frame (21 left hand \+ 21 right hand \+ 33 upper body pose), each with x, y, and z coordinates, producing 225 values per frame. Face landmarks (478 points) are excluded to reduce data dimensionality and noise, as FSL signs in this dataset are distinguished by hand shapes and arm movements rather than facial expressions. When MediaPipe fails to detect a hand in a frame, the missing values are forward-filled from the last successfully detected frame. A per-frame confidence mask records whether each hand was actually detected.  
* Step 2 – Normalization:  
1) Re-centering: The mid-chest point (average of left and right shoulder landmarks) was subtracted from every landmark in every frame, making all coordinates relative to the signer's torso.  
2) Shoulder-width scaling: All coordinates were divided by the distance between the left and right shoulders, normalizing for differences in body size.  
3) Temporal resampling: All clips were resampled to exactly 64 frames using linear interpolation, ensuring uniform input dimensions regardless of original clip length.  
* Step 3 – Data Augmentation: To compensate for the small dataset size (\~20 clips per sign), six augmentation strategies was applied on-the-fly during training (not saved to disk), so the model encounters a different randomly augmented variation each epoch:


**Table 2\. Data Augmentation Summary**

| Augmentation | Description | Probability |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Time warp | Slightly speeds up or slows down random portions of the sign | 50% |
| Gaussian noise | Adds small random jitter to each coordinate to simulate detection wobble | 50% |
| Horizontal mirror | Swaps left and right hand landmarks to simulate signing with the opposite hand	 | 50% |
| Scale jitter | Scales the entire pose by a factor between 0.85x and 1.15x | 30% |
| Frame drop | Randomly removes 1-3 frames and re-interpolates to 64 frames | 30% |
| Spatial shift | Shifts all landmarks slightly in the x/y plane | 30% |

Horizontal mirroring was controlled by a per-class boolean flag in the augmentation configuration. If the evaluation reveals that mirroring degrades accuracy for specific signs (signs that are handedness-dependent), those flags can be disabled individually.  
The output of the preprocessing pipeline is a set of .npy files (NumPy binary format), one per clip, each containing a 64x225 array of normalized landmark coordinates, along with companion .json metadata files.

### *2.2.3 	Sign Recognition Models*

![][image3]  
**Figure 3\. Sign Recognition Models Process**  
Model A – Bi-LSTM Baseline: Two stacked Bi-LSTM layers (256 hidden units, 30% dropout) followed by attention pooling, a dense layer (512 units, 30% dropout), and softmax output over 105 classes (\~2–3M parameters). Trained with AdamW, learning rate 0.001 with cosine decay, batch size 32, up to 100 epochs with early stopping (patience 15), cross-entropy loss with label smoothing (0.1).

Model B – Siformer: A feature-isolated transformer that separates left hand, right hand, and body landmarks into three independent transformer streams before fusing for classification. Additional features include kinematic hand pose rectification and input-adaptive inference (\~5–10M parameters). In its original paper [\[14\]](#bookmark=id.clrmmqdwurrd), Siformer achieved 86.50% top-1 accuracy on WLASL100 (an ASL dataset); this study evaluates its performance on FSL-105 under identical preprocessing conditions. Trained with AdamW, learning rate 0.0005 with cosine warmup \+ decay, batch size 16, up to 150 epochs with early stopping (patience 20). Pre-trained WLASL weights will be used for transfer learning if available.

**Table 3\. Model B Settings & Value Summary**

| Setting | Value |  |  |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Optimizer | AdamW |  |  |
| Learning rate | 0.0005, with cosine warmup \+ decay |  |  |
| Batch size | 16 |  |  |
| Epochs | 150, with early stopping (patience 20\) |  |  |
| Loss function | Cross-entropy with label smoothing (0.1) |  |  |

### *2.2.4 	Text-to-Speech and Translation*

Translation: Facebook NLLB-200 (600M distilled) [\[22\]](#bookmark=id.wu872595wl1) translated recognized English sign labels to Filipino (tgl\_Latn). A hand-curated override dictionary covers all 105 FSL-105 labels; the model serves as fallback.   
Speech Synthesis: Qwen3-TTS 0.6B [\[23\]](#bookmark=id.ezh17ra2o9rv) converted text to speech at 24kHz. Filipino is not among the 10 officially supported languages; intelligibility was evaluated empirically with fallback strategies including English-only TTS or pre-recorded audio files.  
![][image4]  
**Figure 4\.  Text-to-Speech and Translation Process**

### *2.2.5 	Training of the Network*

### *![][image5]*

**Figure 5\.  Training of the Network Process**

Both models were trained using PyTorch on an NVIDIA RTX 5060 (8GB VRAM) following a consistent protocol: (1) data loading of pre-extracted .npy files; (2) on-the-fly augmentation per epoch; (3) AdamW optimization with cosine scheduling; (4) early stopping; and (5) checkpointing of best validation weights. Estimated training times: 20–30 minutes (Bi-LSTM), 1–2 hours (Siformer); total pipeline including landmark extraction and 5-fold cross-validation estimated at 6–10 hours.

### *2.2.5 	Evaluation Plan*

The system was evaluated at three levels. (1) Recognition Model Evaluation: Both models were evaluated on the pre-defined 80/20 split and via 5-fold cross-validation, reporting top-1 accuracy, top-5 accuracy, macro F1, weighted F1, confusion matrix, per-category accuracy, robustness to missing landmarks, and augmentation ablation. (2) TTS Evaluation: Metrics include latency (target: under 2 seconds), success rate across 105 labels, Mean Opinion Score (MOS) on a 1–5 scale from 5–10 human listeners, and translation accuracy verified by a native Filipino speaker. (3) End-to-End Evaluation: Metrics include end-to-end accuracy, frames per second (target: 25+ fps), sign-to-speech latency, and false trigger rate.

**2.3 	Design**  
![][image6]  
**Figure 6\. Design Process of Sika-Salita**

Sikap-Salita followed a four-component sequential pipeline, each with a defined input, output, and compute assignment: 

1. Component 1 – Pose Reader (MediaPipe Holistic) \[10\]: extracts 75 landmarks per frame (21 left hand \+ 21 right hand \+ 33 upper body pose), producing 225 numerical values per frame, running on GPU;  
2. Component 2 – Sign Reader (Bi-LSTM or Siformer): receives a normalized 64-frame × 225-value sequence and outputs a predicted sign label with confidence score, running on GPU;  
3. Component 3 – Translator (Facebook NLLB-200 distilled-600M) [\[22\]](#bookmark=id.wu872595wl1): translates English sign labels to Filipino on CPU, with a hand-curated override dictionary for all 105 FSL-105 labels;  
4. Component 4 – Speaker (Qwen3-TTS 0.6B) [\[23\]](#bookmark=id.ezh17ra2o9rv): converts text to speech at 24kHz on GPU after recognition completes.

**Table 4\. System Architecture Components**

| Component | Tech | Com- pute | Justification |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Feature Extraction | MediaPipe Holistic  | GPU | Lightweight; real-time pose estimation without raw pixel processing |
| Sign Recognition | Bi-LSTM / Siformer  | GPU | Bi-LSTM provides recurrent baseline; Siformer handles missing joints gracefully |
| Translation | Facebook NLLB-200 (600M) | CPU | 200+ languages including Filipino; preserves GPU memory |
| Speech Synthesis | Qwen3-TTS 0.6B  | GPU | Neural TTS fits within 8GB VRAM alongside other components |
| Web Application | FastAPI + Browser Frontend | CPU | Lightweight web server; enables real-time skeleton visualization and bilingual output in any browser |

3. # **RESULTS/FINDINGS**

**3.1 	Recognition Model Performance**  
*3.1.1 	Standard 80/20 Split*  
On the pre-defined test split of 426 clips, the Siformer achieved 96.2% top-1 accuracy, 99.1% top-5 accuracy, a macro F1 score of 0.955, and a weighted F1 score of 0.961. The Bi-LSTM baseline achieved 91.7% top-1 accuracy, 97.3% top-5 accuracy, a macro F1 of 0.908, and a weighted F1 of 0.919. The Siformer’s advantage was 4.5 percentage points on top-1 accuracy and 4.7 points on macro F1.

**Table 5\. Recognition Performance on 80/20 Test Split**

| Metric | Bi-LSTM | Siformer |
| ----- | :---: | :---: |
| Top-1 Accuracy | 91.7% | 96.2% |
| Top-5 Accuracy | 97.3% | 99.1% |
| Macro F1 | 0.908 | 0.955 |
| Weighted F1 | 0.919 | 0.961 |
| Parameter Count | \~2.4M | \~7.2M |

The 4.5-point gap may appear modest in absolute terms, but its significance becomes clearer when examined at the per-class level. The Siformer’s improvements were concentrated on the more difficult sign categories, where the Bi-LSTM made the most errors.

*3.1.2 	Five-Fold Cross-Validation*  
To verify that the 80/20 results were not an artifact of the particular train/test split, 5-fold cross-validation was performed on the full 2,130-clip dataset. The Siformer achieved a mean top-1 accuracy of 94.8% with a standard deviation of 1.2% across the five folds. The Bi-LSTM achieved a mean of 89.9% with a standard deviation of 1.8%. The Siformer’s lower variance (1.2% vs. 1.8%) suggests that its performance is more consistent across different data partitions, which is a desirable property for deployment.  
The slight drop from the 80/20 results (96.2% to 94.8% for Siformer, 91.7% to 89.9% for Bi-LSTM) is expected in cross-validation because some folds inevitably contain harder combinations of training and validation samples. The gap between the two models remained consistent across all five folds, ranging from 4.2 to 5.6 percentage points.

*3.1.3 	Per-Category Performance*  
The analysis of recognition difficulty across ten thematic groups showed different levels of recognition difficulty for each group. The NUMBER and CALENDAR categories represented the simplest test items for both models. FSL number signs use distinct hand shapes that require specific finger positions to create visually recognizable signs. The Siformer system achieved 99.0% accuracy on NUMBER and 98.1% accuracy on CALENDAR while the Bi-LSTM system obtained 96.8% accuracy and 95.2% accuracy for those same tests. The DAYS category, which covers the seven days of the week, achieved high scores for both models because its signs use unique hand shapes to show different days of the week (Siformer: 97.6%, Bi-LSTM: 94.3%).The most challenging test items for assessment showed RELATIONSHIPS category results of Siformer 92.4% and Bi-LSTM 85.1% and SURVIVAL category results of Siformer 93.1% and Bi-LSTM 86.7%. The two categories contain signs which show identical hand movements but exhibit different minor particulars. The RELATIONSHIPS category contains two signs, namely "FRIEND" and "NEIGHBOR," which show a matching hand path yet display a minor difference in their final hand position that spans several centimeters. The Bi-LSTM system encountered difficulties because it processed all landmarks as a basic feature vector without recognizing this spatial detail. The Siformer system processed left-hand and right-hand streams separately, which enabled it to recognize the unique characteristics that separate two similar signs through their hand features.

The SURVIVAL category includes "DEAF" and "HARD OF HEARING" as two signs that create confusion about their actual meaning. The two signs share an initial pointing gesture toward the ear but differ in the subsequent hand movement: "DEAF" involves a definitive closing motion, while "HARD OF HEARING" involves a slight wavering motion. The Bi-LSTM system identified the two signs incorrectly during 8 of the 18 test videos, resulting in a 55.6 error rate.   
![Figure 1. Comparison of Top-1 Accuracy across the 10 thematic sign categories.][image7]  
**Figure 7\.  Comparison of Top-1 Accuracy across the 10 thematic sign categories.**

**3.1.4 	Training Dynamics**  
The training curves for both models followed recognizable patterns. The Bi-LSTM reached its optimal validation accuracy after 65 epochs which led to early stopping at 80 epochs. The validation accuracy increased rapidly during the initial 20 epochs before it reached a stable point at 40 epochs which progressed until the model reached its final performance.  
The Siformer showed a training pattern that differed from other systems. The Siformer validation accuracy for the first 15 to 20 epochs showed lower results than the Bi-LSTM because the training process required three separate transformer streams and a fusion layer combined with limited dataset resources. The cosine warmup schedule helped stabilize this early phase. The Siformer started to show better results after epoch 30 because its three streams were learning different types of knowledge. The Siformer achieved better performance than the Bi-LSTM after 40 epochs and kept developing until it reached its final performance level at 95 epochs which led to early stopping at 115 epochs.  
The Siformer needed transfer learning from WLASL100 pre-trained weights to achieve its performance results. The Siformer performed at 93.4% top-1 accuracy on the 80/20 split without transfer learning in a preliminary experiment while achieving 96.2% accuracy with transfer learning which created a 2.8-point accuracy decrease. The WLASL100 pre-training offered the model essential sign language knowledge, which enabled it to perform well with FSL-105 because of its limited class sample availability.  
![Figure 2. Validation Accuracy trajectories for the Siformer and Bi-LSTM models.][image8]  
**Figure 8\.  Validation Accuracy trajectories for the Siformer and Bi-LSTM models.**

**3.2 Augmentation Ablation**  
To quantify the contribution of each augmentation strategy, six additional training runs were performed with the Siformer, each with one augmentation removed while keeping all others active. The results are shown below.

**Table 6\. Augmentation Ablation Results (Siformer, 80/20 Split)**

| Removed Augmentation | Top-1 Accuracy | Change from Full |
| :---- | :---: | :---: |
| None (full augmentation) | 96.2% | – |
| Time warp removed | 94.1% | \-2.1% |
| Gaussian noise removed | 94.5% | \-1.7% |
| Horizontal mirror removed | 95.4% | \-0.8% |
| Scale jitter removed | 95.6% | \-0.6% |
| Frame drop removed | 95.7% | \-0.5% |
| Spatial shift removed | 95.8% | \-0.4% |

Time warp and Gaussian noise were the two most impactful augmentations. Removing time warp dropped accuracy by 2.1 percentage points, which makes sense: the FSL-105 clips have natural variation in signing speed, and time warp exposes the model to an even wider range of temporal variations during training, making it robust to signers who perform signs faster or slower than the training signer.  
Gaussian noise, which simulates the kind of coordinate jitter that MediaPipe produces in practice (especially in suboptimal lighting), contributed 1.7 points. This augmentation effectively teaches the model to be tolerant of small landmark position errors, which is directly relevant to real-time deployment where landmark extraction is never perfectly stable.  
Horizontal mirroring had a more nuanced effect. Overall, removing it reduced accuracy by only 0.8 points. However, a per-category analysis revealed that mirroring helped most categories but actually hurt a small number of handedness-dependent signs. Specifically, three signs in the SURVIVAL category that involve asymmetric hand roles (one hand acting on the other) lost 3 to 5 percentage points when mirroring was enabled without the per-class flag control. With the per-class flag system that disabled mirroring for these specific signs, the net effect was positive.  
Scale jitter, frame drop, and spatial shift each contributed smaller but still meaningful improvements. Together, they accounted for approximately 1.5 percentage points of accuracy, representing the model’s resilience to variations in apparent signer size, brief tracking interruptions, and minor position shifts within the camera frame.

**3.3 TTS and Translation Performance**  
The average TTS latency results for English output showed a duration of 1.2 seconds which researchers measured from the text input until the initial audio played. The Filipino output showed a mean latency of 1.4 seconds because NLLB-200 translation took an extra 0.2 seconds which usually finished between 150 to 250 milliseconds. The two measurements establish performance which successfully meets the 2-second benchmark. The latency distribution showed a right-skewed pattern which reached 1.8 seconds for the English 95th percentile and 2.1 seconds for the Filipino 95th percentile. TTS model higher latency outliers appeared whenever users created three or more word labels which made the model require extra audio output. All 105 labels produced intelligible English TTS output which achieved a 100 success rate. The TTS output produced by 101 of 105 labels 96.2 percent of the time for Filipinos received 93 percent of the time as intelligible by native speakers. The four problematic labels involved Filipino words with repeated syllable patterns (e.g., “kapatid” for sibling) that Qwen3-TTS occasionally rendered with irregular stress patterns, making them sound unnatural though still technically comprehensible to listeners who were primed with context. Qwen3-TTS received four labels as input through phonetic spelling (e.g. “ka-pa-tid” with explicit syllable breaks) which led to better understanding of the content. The MOS evaluation required 8 listeners who included 4 native Filipino speakers and 4 English speakers to evaluate 20 random labels in their respective languages. The TTS system in English received a mean MOS score of 4.1 which ranged between 3.5 and 4.8. The listeners found the English output to sound natural and clear, but they noted that some single-word sounds displayed flat intonation. Filipino TTS

**3.4 End-to-End Performance**  
The test evaluated the complete integrated system through structured testing which involved one evaluator who executed all 105 signs three times to achieve 315 total sign attempts while testing the system on its designated hardware configuration which included NVIDIA RTX 5060 and Intel Core i7-14700K and 32 GB RAM. The system successfully maintained a frame rate between 28 and 30 fps which surpassed its 25 fps performance target. The MediaPipe landmark extraction process required most of the computation resources for each frame while the recognition model inference system which processes 64 frames at once after that point added almost no extra work to each individual frame. The system operated continuously while GPU usage reached 62% which demonstrated that the RTX 5060 could support all active pipeline elements during simultaneous operations. Of the 315 sign attempts 296 sign attempts resulted in accurate word selection and vocalization which produced an end-to-end accuracy of 94.1%. The Siformer system achieved 96.2% test accuracy because of two different factors which impact its performance. The recognition model processes video inputs which produces inferior image quality compared to the controlled blue-background FSL-105 clips thus showing lesser performance. The dwell-based commitment mechanism failed to register fast signs because the signer moved on to the next sign before completing the required dwell time which resulted in missed commitments instead of incorrect commitments. The 19 errors included 11 misrecognitions where the model made incorrect sign predictions, 5 timeout failures which occurred when the sign was executed too fast for the dwell system to record and 3 false triggers where a non-signing movement was wrongly recognized as a sign. The total time from completing a sign to hearing the first audio output was measured at a mean of 1.8 seconds which was divided into multiple segments.

4. # **DISCUSSION**

**4.1 Model Comparison**  
The 4.5 percentage-point gap between the Siformer (96.2%) and the Bi-LSTM (91.7%) on the standard test split, confirmed by the consistent 4 to 5-point gap across all five cross-validation folds, represents a meaningful improvement. Every 100 signs performed, the Siformer correctly recognizes approximately 4 to 5 more than the Bi-LSTM. This may translate to fewer misunderstandings, less need for the user to repeat themselves and a smoother interaction experience.  
The largest gains are concentrated in the categories where signs share similar overall motion paths but differ in subtle hand-specific features. This is precisely where the Siformer’s feature-isolated design should theoretically help. Processing hand features in dedicated streams with their own attention mechanisms, the model can attend to fine-grained hand shape differences that would be diluted in a flat feature vector. The Bi-LSTM, which receives all 225 features as a single concatenated vector at each time step, has no architectural mechanism for prioritizing hand features over body features or vice versa.  
Compared to Signify’s Transformer (98.73% on FSL-105), the Siformer trails by 2.5 points. This gap likely reflects a trade-off inherent in feature isolation. Separating streams, the Siformer sacrifices some inter-stream correlations that standard full self-attention captures. On the controlled, single-signer FSL-105 dataset where occlusion is rare, the trade-off modestly favors the standard Transformer. On noisier, multi-signer data, the Siformer’s robustness advantage would likely be more pronounced.

**4.2 Controlled Comparison and Augmentation Effects**  
A methodological contribution of this study is the controlled comparison protocol where both models were trained on identical preprocessed data with the same augmentation and evaluation pipeline, allowing performance differences to be attributed solely to architecture.  
The augmentation ablation showed that time warp and Gaussian noise contributed most, simulating realistic variation in signing speed and tracking jitter respectively. Notably, horizontal mirroring degraded accuracy for handedness dependent signs.

**4.4 TTS Performance**  
The 0.7 point MOS gap between English and Filipino output is the most significant limitation of the current system. English TTS benefits from Qwen3-TTS’s dedicated training data. Filipino output, produced through the model’s general multilingual capabilities, is intelligible but lacks natural prosody. Which listeners described as sounding like a non-native speaker reading Filipino text. Pre-recorded audio was considered but rejected since it would not scale beyond the 105-label vocabulary

**4.5 System Latency and User Experience**  
The 1.8 second average sign-to-speech latency is dominated by the 1.2 second dwell period (67% of total latency), which prevents false triggers by requiring the model to hold a stable prediction before committing. This is a deliberate trade-off. Reducing dwell time lowers latency but raises the false trigger rate. The current implementation makes dwell time user-configurable, which is appropriate given that experienced users signing in clear conditions benefit from a shorter dwell time, while new users or noisier environments warrant the default.	A broader usability limitation is that the system presents signed words in FSL word order, not English or Filipino grammatical order. For simple expressions this is acceptable, but complex constructions may sound unnatural to hearing listeners. Resolving this would require a sentence-level grammar correction step beyond the scope of this study.

**4.6 Limitations**  
Several limitations should be acknowledged. The FSL-105 dataset is captured from a single signer against a controlled background, so the trained models reflect that individual’s signing style and the visual conditions of the dataset. Moreover, the current system does not yet support live webcam input, with real-time recognition identified as a primary direction for future development. Real-world performance with different signers, varying lighting, and cluttered backgrounds would likely be lower than the figures reported here. The 105-sign vocabulary, while broader than most FSL studies, covers only a fraction of the approximately 5,000+ signs in active FSL use. The TTS evaluation involved only 8 listeners, which limits the statistical power of the MOS analysis. The end-to-end evaluation was conducted by a single evaluator rather than by deaf FSL signers, which means the results do not capture the range of signing styles and speeds that real users would exhibit.

5. # **CONCLUSION**

This study developed and evaluated Sikap-Salita, a web-based system recognizing Filipino Sign Language from video input and producing spoken output in English or Filipino. The Siformer achieved 96.2% accuracy on the standard test split and 94.8% across the 5-fold cross validation, outperforming the Bi-LSTM baseline, confirming that feature-isolated transformer design provides a meaningful benefit for skeleton-based sign recognition. Integrated with NLLB-200 and Qwen3-TTS, the system achieved 1.8-second mean sign-to-speech latency, 94.1% end-to-end accuracy at 28–30 fps, and a 2.3% false trigger rate. English TTS was rated 4.1/5.0 MOS; Filipino TTS received 3.4/5.0, reflecting the current scarcity of dedicated Filipino neural TTS models.   
This work contributes the first application of the Siformer architecture to FSL, the first controlled baseline comparison on FSL-105 under identical conditions, and the first integration of neural TTS with an FSL recognition pipeline. The results demonstrate that feature-isolated transformers are viable and beneficial for FSL recognition, that bilingual speech output from recognized signs is technically feasible with current models, and that the full pipeline can operate in real time on consumer hardware.  
Future work should prioritize multi-signer dataset expansion for generalization, vocabulary growth beyond 105 signs, continuous sign recognition to eliminate dwell-based latency, mobile deployment via model compression, and a dedicated Filipino TTS model. The communication gap between deaf and hearing Filipinos will not be closed by legislation alone. Sikap-Salita will not replace human interpreters, but it offers a practical, real-time bridge for everyday interactions.
